newsitem.title: USA: Reader's Digest slumps after Q3 earnings.
newsitem.headline: Reader's Digest slumps after Q3 earnings.

text.p: Reader's Digest Association Inc's stock hit a 52-week low on Wednesday as its third quarter earnings dropped and it announced plans to spend $400 million over four years to promote its line of products.
Analysts said they were skeptical that the added investment would address the root of the company's problem: slumping revenues among each of its segments and in all geographic areas.
"This is not a special program," Josephthal Lyon & Ross analyst Dennis McAlpine said. "This is just saying our costs are going up."
In afternoon trading Reader's Digest stock had dropped 2-3/8 to 23-5/8. By early afternoon, more than 630,000 shares had been traded.
The company's third quarter earnings dropped 31 percent, and it offered a forecast for the year that was below analysts' estimates.
For the third quarter ended March 31, Reader's Digest reported net income of $37.6 million, or $0.35 per share, on revenues of $684.3 million.
In the prior year's third quarter, the company reported net income of $55.8 million, or $0.51 per share, on revenue of $747.5 million.
It said it expected its earnings for the full year ending June 30 to be about $1.70 per share. The First Call analysts' mean estimate for the year was $2.15 per share.

Reader's Digest, the publisher and direct marketer of magazines, books, music, videos and new media products, also said it planned to spend $400 million over four years for a variety of promotional initiatives.
Those initiatives include identifying consumer interests, retaining existing customers, tapping into new and younger customers and making selective price reductions.
"There's a concern that the money's not going to be effective," Argus Research analyst John Eade said. "It's a confidence issue. Investors don't have confidence in Reader's Digest management."

Analysts said Reader's Digest has made some strategic missteps, including oversaturing the European market with direct mail and having difficulty in filling some orders after restructuring cutbacks that took place about a year ago.
"They kind of burned out their customers" with too many mailings offering too many products in too short a time, Edward Jones analyst Linda Bannister said.
For the third quarter, revenue at Reader's Digest magazine dropped one percent, books and home entertainment products were down 11 percent and special interest magazines decreased 22 percent.
In the U.S., revenues were down two percent, while European revenues dropped 16 percent, and Pacific and other markets decreased three percent.
"This is what used to be a 15 percent grower with cash in the bank that has changed dramatically," McAlpine said, adding, "They've made a number of wrong assumptions."
Bannister said the company sought to outline its strategy in a call with analysts on Wednesday and had earlier forecast its third quarter earnings.

"But they didn't really give any detail," she said. "They're making strikes in the right direction. But no one really knows what exactly is going to work. ... No one really knows when this is going to turn."
